title: Computer File Paths
summary: Explains what a file path is, the difference between absolute paths (measured from the drive root) and relative paths (measured from the file you are editing), and the two special path tokens ./ and ../. The exercise has learners display five animal images stored in a deliberately tangled folder tree using only relative src paths.

concepts.heading: What a file path is
points: A file path is an address that points to exactly one file or folder in the computer's storage. It is written as a chain of folder names separated by slashes, ending at the target.
Comparable to giving street directions: country, then city, then district, then street, then building. Each step narrows the location until it is unique.
Everyday users rarely type paths because the file browser (Finder / Explorer) lets them click through folders. A path is the text version of that same clicking journey.
The destination of a path can be a file (cat.png, index.html) or a folder (Images/).

concepts.heading: The root of the file system
points: The root is the top of the storage tree, i.e. the hard drive itself: C: on Windows, Macintosh HD on a Mac.
Every folder and file on the machine sits somewhere underneath the root, so the root is the natural starting point for an absolute path.

concepts.heading: Absolute file paths
points: An absolute path starts at the root and lists every folder down to the target, e.g. Windows: C:\Project\Images\cat.png, Mac: /Project/Images/cat.png.
Windows separates folders with backslashes and names the drive letter; macOS/Linux use forward slashes and a leading / for the root.
Because it always begins at the root, an absolute path works no matter which folder or file you are currently in.
Downside for websites: if the project folder is moved, renamed, or put on another machine/server, every absolute path breaks.

concepts.heading: Relative file paths (the one used in web development)
points: A relative path is measured from the location of the file containing the code (e.g. the index.html you are writing in), not from the root.
Example tree: Project/ contains index.html, dog.png and Images/cat.png. From index.html the cat is simply Images/cat.png: go into Images, then pick cat.png.
Relative paths are usually shorter than absolute ones.

Key advantage: they survive moves. If the whole Project folder is nested inside another folder or copied to a server, the internal journey from index.html to Images/cat.png is unchanged, so the links still work.
Use relative paths whenever a page refers to your own resources: images, audio, video, or other HTML pages.

concepts.heading: Special characters: ../ (parent folder)
points: Two dots followed by a slash at the start of a relative path mean: climb out of the current folder to the one above it, then continue from there.
Example: index.html lives in Project/, and essay.docx lives in the root above Project. From index.html the path is ../essay.docx: up one level into the root, then the file.
../ can be repeated to climb more than one level (../../file).
After climbing you can go back down into other folders: ../Folder1/fish.png means up one, then into Folder1, then fish.png.

concepts.heading: Special characters: ./ (current folder)
points: A single dot followed by a slash means: start in the folder that directly contains the current file (the current directory).
Example: index.html and dog.png are both in Project/, so ./dog.png reaches the dog from index.html.
Anything at the same level of the tree as the current file can be reached with ./name.

The ./ can be left off (dog.png works the same in most cases) and you will see that style in other people's code. The course recommends always writing ./ because the shortened form does not resolve correctly in every environment.

(Extra) The browser treats a path with no prefix as relative to the current document's folder, so ./dog.png and dog.png resolve to the same URL; tooling such as JavaScript module imports and some bundlers do require the explicit ./ though, which is why the habit is worth forming.

concepts.heading: Working out where a file sits in VS Code
points: To find which folder contains a file, collapse folders in the Explorer sidebar. If collapsing a folder hides the file, that folder is its parent. If the file stays visible after collapsing everything, it lives in the top-level project folder.
Start typing a path inside src="" and VS Code's autocomplete lists the files and folders reachable from that point. Selecting from the dropdown avoids typos (a single extra letter breaks the path).

Use the suggestions as a sanity check: if the dropdown does not show the folder you expect (e.g. typing ../ when you meant ./ lists dog.png, Folder0 and Folder1 instead of Folder3), the path prefix is wrong.
In the preview, a broken-image icon means the path does not point at a real file; rethink the path rather than the img tag.

concepts.heading: Reminder on the img element
points: Images are added with the self-closing element; src holds the path to the image and alt holds a text description.
Always add alt text so screen-reader users and anyone whose image fails to load still know what the picture shows.

Root (C:  or  Macintosh HD)
├── essay.docx
└── Project/
    ├── index.html      <- you are writing code here
    ├── dog.png
    └── Images/
        └── cat.png

Absolute (Windows):  C:\Project\Images\cat.png
Absolute (Mac):      /Project/Images/cat.png
Relative from index.html:
  Images/cat.png      (or ./Images/cat.png)
  ./dog.png           same folder as index.html
  ../essay.docx       up one level to the root

task.name: 4.0 File Paths: All the Animals
task.starting_point: Folder0/index.html contains an h1 'All the Animals' and five h2 headings (Rabbit:, Cat:, Dog:, Fish:, Bird:) with nothing under them. The five images are scattered across the folder tree shown above, and goal.png shows the finished page.
task.goal: Under each h2, add an img whose src is a relative path from Folder0/index.html to the correct animal picture, so every image displays as in goal.png.
steps: Extract the download, open it inside the Web Development Projects folder in VS Code, and expand every folder so the full tree is visible.
Rabbit (easiest, same folder as index.html): .
Cat (one folder down): start in the current folder, go into Folder3, pick the file: ./Folder3/cat.png.
Dog (in the top-level exercise folder): collapse folders to confirm dog.png sits directly in 4.0 File Paths. From Folder0 climb one level with ../ and select the file: ../dog.png.
Fish: climb out of Folder0, then go into its sibling Folder1: ../Folder1/fish.png.
Bird: same route as the fish, one folder deeper: ../Folder1/Folder2/bird.png (copy the fish path and extend it).
Give every img an alt attribute naming the animal and close each with the self-closing />.
Use VS Code's path autocomplete while typing each src, and check the preview after each image; a broken-image icon means the path is wrong.
Compare with goal.png and then with solution.html.
task.expected_result: The page shows the heading 'All the Animals' followed by Rabbit, Cat, Dog, Fish and Bird, each with its photo underneath and no broken-image icons.

pitfalls: Confusing ./ with ../: ./ stays in the folder that holds the current file; ../ climbs one level above it. The lecture sometimes phrases ./ as moving 'up to the parent folder', meaning the folder that contains index.html, not the one above it.
Measuring the path from the project root or from where the image 'feels' it should be, rather than from the HTML file being edited.
Typos in folder or file names (one extra letter breaks the path). Prefer selecting from VS Code's autocomplete.
Using absolute paths like C:\Users\...\cat.png in a web page: they only work on your own machine and break once the site is moved or deployed.
Leaving out alt text on the images.
